newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Rwanda opposes intervention in eastern Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda opposes intervention in eastern Zaire.

text.p: Rwandan Foreign Minister Anastase Gasana said on Tuesday Rwanda would strongly oppose any international military intervention in eastern Zaire to aid hundreds thousands of refugees fleeing from fighting there.
"If there were a decision for such an intervention...it would be opposed by the sub-region by all means, not only political," he told a news conference at the Rwandan embassy in Brussels.

According to Gasana, Rwanda and neighbouring Burundi -- both ruled by ethnic Tutsis -- and eastern Zaire, where Banyamulenge Tutsis settled from Rwanda 200 years ago, form a subregion in the central African Great Lakes area.
"The Rwandan government has an obvious interest in eastern Zaire," Gasana said.

Caught up in the battles are more than one million refugees from Rwanda, but also Burundi. The bulk of them are Hutus who have fled ethnic conflict with Tutsis. Some left their country in fear of reprisals after mass killings of Tutsis.
France and Spain want the idea of a multi-national force to be considered to guarantee distribution of humanitarian aid to the refugees.

Gasana denied international aid organisation reports that Rwandan troops were involved in fighting between Banyamulenge Tutsi rebels and the Zairean army in the area and indicated no troops would sent across the border with Zaire.
Rwanda had no territorial claims on eastern Zaire nor did it have "special links" with the Banyamulenge, he said.
Gasana said: "We wish that in spite of everything (the refugees) return to Rwanda. The Rwandan government is ready to do everything to facilitate the return of the refugees."

"The refugees are prisoners of the Zairean army, of the Zairean authority, of the militia, of the RPR (the former Rwandan army), they are being held hostage, held by those responsible for the 1994 genocide," he said.
Saying the refugees "have become a political trump card," he accused those holding them of forcing the refugees west to prevent their return to Rwanda from eastern Zaire.

Gasane's view of recent events in the region differs from that of political analysts who have said that Rwanda is seeking to drive the Hutu refugees farther from its borders to create a safety buffer zone and prevent their return.

The analysts say that to remove any threat to the government of minority Tutsis, Kigali has actively been supporting Banyamulenge rebels which are currently battling notoriously undisciplined Zairean forces.
Kigali's official standpoint is that it is sympathtic to the Banyamulenge's plight, but regards their conflict with Kinshasha as an internal Zairean affair.

Analysts have also said that under any regional pact on the conflict Rwanda's Tutsi army will insist the rebels' military gains in eastern Zaire are not jeopardised by any foreign intervention to help the refugees.

Gasana said he was suspicious of foreign troops intervening in the conflict, recalling French military intervention, codenamed Operation Turquoise, in the wake of the 1994 genocide had enabled many Hutus guilty of the killings to escape justice.
"We mistrust foreign troops in Africa," he said. If there were an international intervention force "to help a dictator like (Zairean president) Mobutu (Sese Seko), we would oppose."
"The situation in Zaire is a product of Operation Turquoise which allowed criminals and armed soldiers to hide among innocent refugees," the minister said.
He said the Banyamulenge were fighting for survival after Zaire ordered their expulsion from the country and "plans their extermination."
